The missing feature is a warn-instead-of-die mode over a declarative incompatibility table.

desc: required params: --phyloP without its companion --custom dies with /You must set --\w+ to use --\w+/
rationale: The specific pair is out of scope -- vepyr has no custom annotation and no phyloP, see row 22 -- but the rule the Perl regex pins is generic: an option that requires a companion is REFUSED without it, by a message naming both. vepyr carries exactly one such pair and cites VEP for it: `validate_hgvs_reference_fasta` (dfbf 391f94bd `annotate_provider.rs:3637-3648`, doc comment at `:3628-3630` citing Runner.pm#L726-L738) refuses HGVS output when `reference_fasta_path` is unset, with `annotate_vep(): Cannot generate HGVS coordinates (--hgvs/--hgvsc/--hgvsp) without reference_fasta_path (VEP --fasta)`. Analog, not unit: a different option pair, and the refusal is observed as a failed run rather than as a constructor that dies. What made it `blocked-data` under issue 76 is that the check fires during the SCAN (`:5266`, from `scan_with_transcript_engine_partitioned` at `:5203`), not at planning time, so it is unreachable until a run gets that far -- which is why the other four Config rows ported in this file need no fixture and this one needs `tests/data/vep115_parquet_micro_cache/` (issue 96). The positive control is the same request with the companion supplied: it must annotate one row, or `refused` would be indistinguishable from `never worked`. Distinct from BaseVEP.ledger.toml n=22 and n=25, which use the same error family to ask whether a reader EXISTS; this row asks whether the option is refused.

desc: no database/cache/offline: with none of the three sources chosen, VEP dies with /The VEP can read gene data from/
rationale: The pick-one-of-three arm has no counterpart, vepyr having exactly one source of gene data, but the product invariant the assertion protects does: the engine must refuse to run rather than silently emit unannotated output when no source is reachable. `AnnotateFunction::call` resolves the cache's variation manifest at `annotate_table_function.rs:85-87`, before it resolves the VCF table at `:96`, so an absent cache is refused at planning time and the named test drives it with nothing registered at all. Different channel: a missing manifest instead of a missing mode flag.

desc: STDOUT output turns on quiet: output_file = 'STDOUT' forces param('quiet') to 1
rationale: vepyr has no output-target abstraction to special-case. `annotate_to_vcf(input_vcf, cache_source, backend, output_vcf, config)` takes its destination as a path string (`vcf_sink.rs:1018-1024`) with no STDOUT variant, and no `output_file`, `quiet` or `verbose` option exists anywhere in the crate: `grep -rnE '"output_file"|"verbose"|"quiet"|stdout' datafusion/bio-function-vep/src` returns 0 at 391f94bd (positive control: `options_json`, 95 hits). The nearest field, `show_progress` (`vcf_sink.rs:446-448`), draws an indicatif bar on stderr and is never derived from the destination. The missing feature is an output target with a STDOUT variant and the logging rule that follows from it.

desc: STDOUT output turns off verbose: the same STDOUT destination clears an explicitly requested verbose
rationale: The second half of row 34's side effect, blocked by the same absence: with no output target and no `verbose` option (0 hits for either at 391f94bd; positive control `options_json`, 95), there is neither a flag to clear nor an event to clear it on. It is worth keeping distinct from row 34 in review because it is the override direction — an explicit user request being silently revoked — which is the part a future vepyr output-target design would most easily get wrong.

desc: everything with database turns off af_1kg, af_gnomad and pubmed: one statement inside a `for qw(...)` loop, standing for all three options
rationale: A database-mode collapse: `--everything` asks for annotations only the cache can serve, so Config silently drops them when `--database` is on. vepyr has no database mode (row 19; `"database"` 0 hits at 391f94bd), so there is nothing for the collapse to fire against. The pin implements the opposite, cache-mode direction of the same Config.pm block — `af_1kg = everything || parse("af_1kg")`, `pubmed = everything || parse("pubmed")` (`annotate_provider.rs:1176-1181`) — so this row is a feature gap, not a discrepancy: the rule vepyr does implement is the one VEP applies when `--database` is absent.

desc: use test: the Bio::EnsEMBL::VEP::FilterSet module compiles, loads and runs its import at run time
rationale: docs/ledger-contract.md RULING R2 makes use_ok not-applicable unconditionally, and R2's reason applies literally: the line tests Perl's own loader — that require found FilterSet.pm, compiled it and ran its import — and no Rust design contains a runtime module-load assertion that could succeed or fail. Keeping the load probe out of the denominator hides nothing, because the gap is counted by the doing-rows: all 159 remaining rows of this ledger are no-feature and all stay in. Counting the module-load line too would count the same absence twice, once for what the class does and once for the class existing, and would inflate precisely the ledger where the gap is already total. Same idiom and same reading at ledger/Parser_ID.ledger.toml n=1.

desc: new ref: FilterSet->new() called with no filter string still returns a blessed Bio::EnsEMBL::VEP::FilterSet, so an empty filter set is a legal filter set whose filter_root parse_filters() built from an empty argument list
rationale: FILE ANCHOR — the product statement the other 158 no-feature rows cite, with every measurement behind it in this ledger's header. RULING R1 sends this readback to the ok($obj) denotation table rather than to not-applicable, because neither R1 escape holds. (i) The construction is not accounted for elsewhere: `grep -n 'ok($fs' perl/FilterSet.t` returns lines 518 and 522 only, both ontology_* setter probes inside the SKIP block, so this line is the ledger's only accounting for FilterSet->new(). (ii) The class does not denote a capability vepyr has. What it denotes is VEP's filter-expression engine — parse_filters (FilterSet.pm:209) compiles the --filter mini-language into a node tree, evaluate (:441) runs that tree against a flattened annotation hash — serving two callers at release/116.0: the filter_vep script and AnnotationSource::new, which builds a filter_set from a custom source's `filter` key (AnnotationSource.pm:86-89). Neither exists in vepyr at any visibility, so nothing here waits on a `pub` and the denotation table returns no-feature, not deferred/blocked-api (docs/ledger-contract.md, `Absent operation vs present-but-private state`). detailed_plans/FilterSet.md reaches the same verdict independently: EXCLUDE-no-analogue, `vepyr does not filter output`, promotion `requires vepyr to add output filtering as a feature`.

desc: defined_and_non_empty - 1: the scalar 1 counts as present, returning the canonical 1 rather than a bare Perl truth value
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=3-8. defined_and_non_empty (FilterSet.pm:328-330) is the tokenizer's emptiness test, not a general utility: parse_filters' scanner `while($filter_list =~ m/([^\(^\)^\s]*?)(\s|\(|\)|$)/g)` can match an empty word with an empty separator, and :227 ends the iteration only when both are empty, while :238 uses the same predicate to decide that a token is a word at all. So the six rows here pin the boundary between `no token` and `a token that happens to look false`, which is what keeps a filter like `foo eq 0` from being silently dropped during parsing. vepyr has no tokenizer to hold such a boundary, because it has no filter language to tokenise: the engine grep in this ledger's header returns 0 lines across all four dfbf crates at 391f94bd against a 562-line positive control, and defined_and_non_empty specifically is one of the nine names in it. no-feature, per the file anchor at n=2.

desc: defined_and_non_empty - 0: the scalar 0 counts as present (returns 1), so a Perl-false but defined, non-empty token survives tokenisation
rationale: The sharpest row of the family and the reason the method is not just `if($word)`: 0 is false in Perl but is a legal field name character and a legal filter value, so the predicate has to separate falsity from absence — `defined($_[1]) && $_[1] ne ''` (FilterSet.pm:329), never a bare truth test. Read against n=3 it fixes the intent: presence, not truth. Absent for the same reason as the anchor n=3; vepyr parses no filter string, so no code path can hold or violate this distinction.

desc: defined_and_non_empty - string: a non-numeric scalar ('foo') counts as present, so the predicate is type-blind
rationale: Adds the text case to n=3's numeric one, showing the predicate never inspects the token's type — which matters because the same scanner feeds field names, operator words and values through it (FilterSet.pm:227, :238). vepyr has no such scanner: see anchor n=3 and the file anchor n=2.

desc: defined_and_non_empty - empty string: the empty string counts as absent (returns 0), which is how the scanner recognises a zero-width match and stops
rationale: The complement of n=4, and the case that carries the method's operational weight: the regex at FilterSet.pm:223 matches zero-width, so without `ne ''` the parse loop would never terminate. This row pins the loop's exit condition, not a formatting nicety. No vepyr code path can exhibit it, because there is no parse loop — anchor n=3.

desc: defined_and_non_empty - undef: an undefined value counts as absent (returns 0), the `defined` half of the conjunction
rationale: Isolates the first conjunct of FilterSet.pm:329 the way n=6 isolates the second: undef is absent even before the string comparison, which also keeps the `ne ''` from warning under `use warnings` (t/FilterSet.t:16). Absent in vepyr for the anchor's reason, n=3.

desc: defined_and_non_empty - no value: calling the method with no argument at all is the same as passing undef, returning 0 rather than dying
rationale: The arity case: `$_[1]` is simply not there, and the method must be total over that too, because :227 calls it on `$sep` which the regex leaves unset at end of input. Distinct from n=7 in Perl (missing argument versus explicit undef) even though both reach the same branch; the row is here because the enumerator counts statements and this is a separate statement pinning a separate call shape. vepyr has no analogue — anchor n=3.

desc: create_filter_node - no params: a node built from nothing is initialised to {logic => 'and', components => []}, so `and` is the default sibling logic and every node starts childless
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=9-11. create_filter_node (FilterSet.pm:345-353) is the AST constructor of the filter language: it defaults `logic` to and and `components` to an empty list, and parse_filters calls it for the root (:213) and for every word and parenthesis it meets. What the three rows pin is that the default composition of two adjacent filter units is conjunction — the semantics `--filter "a b"` means `a and b` depends on this line alone. vepyr has no AST for filters because it has no filter language: create_filter_node is one of the nine names in the header's engine grep, which returns 0 lines across the four dfbf crates at 391f94bd. no-feature per the file anchor n=2, not blocked-api: there is no private node type waiting to be exported.

desc: create_filter_node - logic: an explicitly supplied {logic => 'or'} survives initialisation instead of being overwritten by the `and` default
rationale: The `unless exists` half of FilterSet.pm:349 — the defaults are defaults, not assignments, which is what lets parse_filters set `or` on a node before handing it to the constructor (:247). Without this row n=9 alone would be satisfied by an unconditional write. Absent in vepyr for the anchor's reason, n=9.

desc: create_filter_node - components: a supplied {components => ['foo']} survives initialisation and still gains the default logic => 'and'
rationale: The same non-overwriting rule as n=10 applied to the other defaulted key (FilterSet.pm:350), plus the mixed case: one key given, one defaulted, in a single call. Together n=9-11 exhaust the constructor's 2x2 behaviour minus the both-given case. No vepyr counterpart — anchor n=9.

desc: finish_filter_node - basic: finalising a bare node assigns the default operator `ex`, so a filter naming only a field means `that field exists`
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=12-20. finish_filter_node (FilterSet.pm:370-424) is the second half of the parser: it defaults the operator to ex (`$filter->{operator} ||= 'ex'`, :374), rewrites value-less comparisons (:381-384), materialises `in` sets from a literal or a file (:385-418), and deletes the `parent` back-pointer (:421). This row pins the default that gives VEP's filter language its terse form — `--filter "CANONICAL"` means `the CANONICAL field is present`, which is the idiom most filter_vep invocations use. vepyr has no operator defaulting because it has no operators: finish_filter_node is one of the nine names in the header's engine grep (0 lines across four crates at 391f94bd, 562-line positive control). no-feature per the file anchor n=2.

desc: finish_filter_node - dont overwrite op: a node that already carries operator => 'gt' keeps it, so the ex default is applied only when no operator was parsed
rationale: The `||=` half of FilterSet.pm:374 read as a guard rather than an assignment, and the row that stops n=12 being satisfiable by an unconditional write. Note the operator is defaulted by Perl truth, so an operator named `0` would also be replaced — a wart with no consequence, since :276 admits only names for which a filter_* sub exists. Absent in vepyr for the anchor's reason, n=12.

desc: finish_filter_node - no value changes op 1: operator `is` with no value collapses to `ex`, so `--filter "foo is"` asks whether foo exists rather than comparing it to nothing
rationale: One of the two value-less rewrites at FilterSet.pm:380-383, and a genuine language rule rather than error handling: VEP accepts a truncated comparison and reinterprets it as an existence test instead of throwing. The pair n=14/n=15 is what makes the rewrite table two rows wide. No vepyr code path can exhibit it — anchor n=12.

desc: finish_filter_node - no value changes op 2: operator `ne` with no value collapses to `nex`, the negated existence test, not to `ex`
rationale: The polarity-preserving half of the same rewrite (FilterSet.pm:381): a truncated negative comparison becomes a negative existence test, so `--filter "foo ne"` means `foo is absent`. Read with n=14 it shows the rewrite is a mapping over operator polarity and not a single fallback, which a Rust reimplementation would have to reproduce operator by operator. Absent in vepyr — anchor n=12.

desc: finish_filter_node - parent gets deleted: the `parent` back-pointer a node carries during parsing is removed on finalisation, leaving an acyclic tree
rationale: The memory-management rule of the AST: parse_filters threads `parent` through nested parentheses (FilterSet.pm:248, :294) and finish_filter_node deletes it (:421) so the finished tree is a DAG Perl's refcounting can free, and so is_deeply comparisons like n=19-20 and n=21-34 can be written against a finite structure at all. A Rust reimplementation would not need the deletion — ownership makes the back-pointer a different problem — but that is an argument about how the absent feature would be built, not evidence it exists. no-feature, anchor n=12.

desc: finish_filter_node - in operator throws on no value: operator `in` with nothing to match against dies with /No list\/file given/
rationale: The first of the family's two throws (FilterSet.pm:389). It pins that `in` is the one operator whose value is mandatory at parse time, because it is the one whose value is a set that has to be materialised before evaluation rather than compared lazily. Classified no-feature rather than not-applicable although the assertion is about a die: what it pins is a product decision — which operators need an eagerly-built operand — and no-feature keeps that in the denominator, the same reading ledger/Parser_ID.ledger.toml n=3 gives a throws_ok. Anchor n=12.

desc: finish_filter_node - in operator throws on invalid value: `in foo`, a value that is neither a comma list nor an existing file, dies with /Could not find\/parse list /
rationale: The second throw (FilterSet.pm:415) and the one that fixes the operand grammar: FilterSet.pm:392 accepts a value matching /.+\,.+/ as a literal list, :396 accepts it as a filename when `-e` says the path exists, and anything else is an error. So `in` has exactly two operand forms and no third fallback — a bare single token is refused rather than treated as a one-element set. Same no-feature reading as n=17; anchor n=12.

desc: finish_filter_node - in operator with list: `in foo,bar` materialises the comma list into the lookup hash {foo => 1, bar => 1}, replacing the string value on the node
rationale: The literal-list branch of FilterSet.pm:392-394, and the row that shows `in` is not a string operator: the node's `value` stops being a string and becomes a hashref, which is what lets filter_in be `exists($_[1]->{$_[0]})` (FilterSet.pm:718) — an O(1) membership test rather than a scan. That representation change is a design decision a port would have to reproduce, and it is what the evaluate-side rows n=126-130 then exercise. Absent in vepyr for the anchor's reason, n=12.

desc: finish_filter_node - in operator with file: `in <path>` reads the fixture list file line by line, stripping CR and vertical whitespace, and materialises it into {MRPL39 => 1, JAM2 => 1}
rationale: The file branch of FilterSet.pm:396-412, and the family's only row that touches the filesystem: the same hash representation as n=19, reached by reading one term per line, with an explicit CR / vertical-whitespace strip whose two arms are chosen on `$]` (:401-406) so DOS-terminated gene lists work on Perl 5.8.8. The fixture is VEPTestingConfig's filter_list, so the row also pins that the operand is a plain newline-separated file with no header and no format detection. vepyr reads gene lists nowhere: the header's engine grep is 0 across four crates and AnnotateVcfConfig's 34 public fields include no list-file path (`awk '/pub struct AnnotateVcfConfig \{/,/^\}/' src/vcf_sink.rs | grep -cE '^    pub [a-z_]*filter'` -> 0). no-feature, anchor n=12.

desc: parse_filters - empty: parsing no filter strings at all still yields a root node {is_root => 1, components => [], logic => 'and'}, so an unfiltered run has a well-formed empty tree rather than undef
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=21-39. parse_filters (FilterSet.pm:209-310) is the compiler of VEP's filter language, and the 19 rows here are its whole specification: a single-regex scanner (`while($filter_list =~ m/([^\(^\)^\s]*?)(\s|\(|\)|$)/g)`, :224) walks one word and one separator at a time, filling each node's field, then operator, then value in that order (:260-286), while `and`/`or` close the current node and open the next (:240-250), `not` flips the current node (:256), and the parenthesis separators push and pop the parent chain (:289-305). This row pins the degenerate case that makes the rest total: an empty argument list still returns the root create_filter_node built at :213, so evaluate always has a tree to walk. vepyr compiles no filter language — parse_filters is one of the nine names in the header's engine grep, 0 lines across all four dfbf crates at 391f94bd against a 562-line positive control — and no private item is standing in the way, so the family is no-feature, not deferred/blocked-api. See the file anchor n=2.

desc: parse_filters - basic: the single word `foo` compiles to one component {field => 'foo', operator => 'ex', logic => 'and', components => []} hanging off the root
rationale: The minimal non-empty parse, and the row that fixes the shape every later expectation in this family is written against: a bare word becomes a *field*, not a value (FilterSet.pm:260-261, the first of the field/operator/value slots), and finish_filter_node then supplies the ex operator (n=12). Absent in vepyr for the anchor's reason, n=21.

desc: parse_filters - basic not: `not foo` compiles to the same single component plus not => 1, so negation is a flag on the node rather than a wrapper node
rationale: The `not` word is handled at FilterSet.pm:253-255 by setting a flag on the *current* node, which is why the expected tree here is n=22's tree with one extra key and not a nested structure. That representation is what lets evaluate invert at :507-508 after the sub-tree has been reduced, and it is the same flag n=33 places on a parenthesised group. No vepyr counterpart — anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - basic, two filters: two separate filter strings ['foo', 'bar'] compile to two sibling components, each with logic => 'and'
rationale: Pins that the argument is a *list* of filter strings and each element gets its own node parented to the root (FilterSet.pm:219-221), i.e. repeating --filter on the command line conjoins. Read against n=28, which compiles the single string 'foo and bar' to a byte-identical tree, the pair says repetition and the `and` keyword are the same operation — a language-level equivalence a reimplementation could easily get wrong in one direction. Absent in vepyr, anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - basic with op and value: `foo eq bar` fills the three slots in order, giving {field => 'foo', operator => 'eq', value => 'bar'}
rationale: The first full triple, and the row that pins the slot *order*: FilterSet.pm:260-286 assigns field if unset, else operator if unset, else value, so position alone decides a word's role and there is no separate lexer class for operators. Note the assertion indexes ->{components}->[0] rather than comparing the whole root, which is how the family narrows from tree shape (n=21-24) to node content. No vepyr analogue — anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - op synonym 1: `foo = bar` parses to operator 'eq', the canonical name, not to '='
rationale: The operator alias table %FILTER_SYNONYMS (FilterSet.pm:100-117) maps 13 spellings onto 7 canonical operators — '>' '>=' '<' '<=' onto gt/gte/lt/lte, 'is' and '=' onto eq, '!=' onto ne, 'exists' and 'defined' onto ex, 'match' 'matches' 'regex' onto re — and :271-273 rewrites the word before it is stored, so the alias never survives into the tree. This row pins the symbolic half of that table; n=27 pins the word half. vepyr has no operator vocabulary to alias — anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - op synonym 2: `foo is bar` also parses to operator 'eq', so `is` is a plain alias for string equality
rationale: The row that corrects detailed_plans/FilterSet.md, which calls `is` the ontology operator. At release/116.0 `is` is entry 'is' => 'eq' in %FILTER_SYNONYMS (FilterSet.pm:106); the ontology operator is the separate `is_child` (FilterSet.pm:722, this ledger n=153-160), and the promotion that would have turned `Consequence eq X` into `is_child` is commented out in finish_filter_node (FilterSet.pm:376-378). So `--filter "Consequence is missense_variant"` is exact string equality against the whole Consequence field, not a hierarchy walk — which also means it does not match `missense_variant&splice_region_variant` except through the &-split path (n=57, n=67). The distinction matters for sizing the absent feature, not for its category: vepyr has neither operator. Anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - two with logic (and): the single string `foo and bar` compiles to two sibling components, both logic => 'and' — the same tree as the two-element list in n=24
rationale: The `and` keyword at FilterSet.pm:240-250: it finishes the current node, pushes it to the parent, and opens a fresh node carrying the keyword as its own logic. Because 'and' is also the create_filter_node default (n=9), this tree is indistinguishable from n=24's, which is the equivalence that pair exists to state. Absent in vepyr — anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - two with logic (or): `foo or bar` gives components [{foo, logic 'and'}, {bar, logic 'or'}] — the connective is stored on the RIGHT operand, not on the parent
rationale: The subtlest structural fact in the parser and the one a reimplementation is most likely to get wrong: FilterSet.pm:246-249 attaches the keyword to the node it *opens*, so a node's `logic` says how it joins to its left sibling. That is why the first component of an `or` expression still reads logic => 'and', and why evaluate's accumulator can be a single left fold (`*=` for and, `+=` for or, :454-459) with no precedence table at all. The consequence is visible at n=138-140, where `foo or bar` returns 2 rather than 1. No vepyr counterpart — anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - two, one short one full 1: `foo eq goo and bar` mixes a three-word comparison with a bare existence test, giving {foo, eq, goo} then {bar, ex}
rationale: Pins that the slot-filling state (n=25) resets at each connective rather than running across the whole string: `and` opens a fresh node whose field slot is empty again (FilterSet.pm:246-249), so `bar` is a field and not the value of the previous comparison. Without this row the parser could satisfy n=25 and n=28 while still leaking state across the connective. Absent in vepyr — anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - two, one short one full 2: `foo and bar eq goo` is the mirror of n=30, giving {foo, ex} then {bar, eq, goo}
rationale: The other order, and it is a distinct claim rather than symmetry for its own sake: here the *first* node is finished with an unfilled operator slot, so finish_filter_node's ex default (n=12) has to fire on a node the scanner left mid-way, while in n=30 it fires on a node opened after the connective. The pair brackets the interaction between the scanner's state machine and the finaliser. No vepyr analogue — anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - parentheses basic: `foo and (bar)` nests, giving a second component with operator 'ex', logic 'and' and its own components [{bar, ex}] — a group node carries no field
rationale: The push half of the parenthesis handling (FilterSet.pm:289-295): '(' makes the current node the parent and opens a fresh child, and ')' finishes the child, pushes it and restores the parent (:297-303). The row's content is that a group is an ordinary node with children instead of a field — which is why it too receives the ex operator default from finish_filter_node, a detail that looks like noise until n=33 hangs a `not` on it. vepyr parses no grouping because it parses no expression — anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - parentheses basic with not: `foo and not (bar or gwar)` puts not => 1 on the group node itself, and the inner `or` still lands on the right-hand child
rationale: Combines n=23's node-level negation flag with n=32's group node and n=29's right-operand logic, and the expected tree shows all three composing without a special case: `not` is set on the node that is current when the word is read (FilterSet.pm:254), which at that moment is the node '(' is about to become the parent of. That is what makes De-Morgan-free evaluation possible — evaluate inverts the reduced sub-tree at :507-508 rather than pushing negation inward. Absent in vepyr — anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - parentheses complex: `foo and (bar or (gwar and char)) or (car and star)` compiles to a three-deep tree, pinning nesting, sibling logic and group-level logic in one expectation
rationale: The family's stress case and its largest expectation: two sibling groups, one of them containing a further group, with `or` appearing both between leaves (gwar/char's sibling) and between groups (the final group's logic => 'or'). It is the only row that shows the parent chain being popped more than one level, which the ')' branch does by assignment rather than by a stack (FilterSet.pm:297-302) — a shortcut that works only because every node keeps its own parent pointer, the pointer n=16 then deletes. No vepyr analogue — anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - incomplete parentheses 1: the lone string `(` dies with /Error parsing filter string.+incomplete parentheses sets/
rationale: First of four balance checks. The parser has no separate validation pass: the only test is that when the scanner reaches end of input the current node's parent is the root (FilterSet.pm:231), which an unclosed '(' violates because '(' has already re-parented. Classified no-feature rather than not-applicable although it asserts a die — what it pins is the language's syntactic contract, and no-feature keeps it in the denominator, the reading ledger/Parser_ID.ledger.toml n=3 gives a throws_ok. Anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - incomplete parentheses 2: `foo and (bar` — an unclosed group with content in it — dies with the same message
rationale: Distinct from n=35 in that the group is non-empty and the string is otherwise well-formed, so the check cannot be a cheap `is the string exactly '('` guard; it has to be the end-of-input parent test at FilterSet.pm:231. Same no-feature reading as n=35, anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - incomplete parentheses 3: the lone string `)` also dies with /incomplete parentheses sets/, so an unmatched close is refused as loudly as an unmatched open
rationale: The opposite imbalance, and the one whose mechanism differs: ')' pops to the current node's parent (FilterSet.pm:297) when there is nothing to pop to, so the end-of-input test at :231 finds no root above it. The message is shared, which is a deliberate upstream choice — one diagnostic for both directions — and worth recording because a reimplementation is likely to produce two. Same no-feature reading as n=35, anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - incomplete parentheses 4: `foo and (bar or (gwar and char) or (car and star)` — deep nesting one close short — dies with the same message
rationale: The check at depth: three groups open, two close, and the imbalance is detected only at end of input rather than at the second ')' — evidence that the parser tracks balance solely through the parent chain and never counts. Rounds out n=35-37 into the four-way balance specification. Anchor n=21.

desc: parse_filters - invalid operator: `foo was bar` dies with /No such operator/, because `was` is neither a filter_* sub nor a %FILTER_SYNONYMS key
rationale: The family's only vocabulary check, and it is done by symbol-table lookup rather than by a list: FilterSet.pm:267-278 builds the name 'filter_'.$word and asks `defined(&$sub_name)`, consulting %FILTER_SYNONYMS only on the miss. So the operator set is exactly the set of filter_* subs the module defines (:704-748), and adding an operator upstream means adding a sub. That makes the closed vocabulary a property of the code rather than of a table, which is precisely the design decision a Rust port would have to replace. no-feature — vepyr has no operator vocabulary at all, closed or open. Anchor n=21.

desc: new with filter: FilterSet->new('foo') returns an object whose ONLY key is filter_root, holding the tree parse_filters built — the constructor stores the parse and nothing else
rationale: Own anchor. The assertion is is_deeply against a `bless(..., 'Bio::EnsEMBL::VEP::FilterSet')` literal, so it is tempting to read it as the blessing probe the contract lists under not-applicable. It is not: because is_deeply compares the whole structure, the discriminating content is the single-key hash, i.e. that new (FilterSet.pm:132-142) delegates entirely to parse_filters and caches no config, no synonyms table and no compiled predicates. The bless merely spells the expected value's class, and n=2 already accounts for class identity. Under the contract's SKIP-convention corollary — a probe belongs to the absent feature when its *subject* is the absent feature — the subject here is the parsed filter tree, so the row stays no-feature and in the denominator. The lazily-created slots this row proves absent (synonyms at :630, limit_synonym_search at :652) are what n=151-152 then exercise. File anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - ex - pass: with the filter `foo`, a record carrying foo => 1 evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=41-44, and the entry point for every evaluate family that follows (n=41-150). evaluate (FilterSet.pm:441-512) walks the tree twice over: a node with children reduces them into an integer accumulator seeded at 1, multiplying for logic 'and' and adding for logic 'or' (:454-459), while a leaf resolves its field through get_input (:472) and calls the predicate named filter_<operator> (:466-467). filter_ex is `defined($_[0])` (:710), so `--filter "foo"` asks only whether the field resolved — and note the Perl boolean the predicate returns becomes an integer only in the parent's accumulator, which is the same mechanism that lets n=138 return 2. vepyr evaluates no predicates over annotation fields: the header's engine grep is 0 lines across four dfbf crates at 391f94bd, and the WHERE-clause channel is not an analogue because AnnotateProvider never overrides supports_filters_pushdown (0 occurrences; positive control: 2 TableProvider impls), so DataFusion's FilterExec, not vepyr, would be under test. no-feature per the file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - ex - pass 0: foo => 0 also evaluates to 1, because existence is `defined`, not Perl truth
rationale: The evaluate-side twin of n=4: a field whose value is 0 exists. It matters in practice because most numeric CSQ fields (DISTANCE, STRAND, allele frequencies) legitimately take 0, and an existence filter built on truthiness would silently drop them. filter_ex is `defined($_[0])` (FilterSet.pm:710) precisely so it cannot. Absent in vepyr for the anchor's reason, n=41.

desc: evaluate - ex - fail missing: a record with no foo key at all evaluates to 0, after the synonym search has failed to find one
rationale: The negative case, and it is not free: get_input (FilterSet.pm:538-583) tries the key, then a memoised synonym, then lc, uc and "_"-prefixed variants, then a unique case-insensitive prefix match over the record's keys, before giving up. So this row asserts the *whole* resolution chain came back empty for a record whose only key is `bar` — a stronger statement than a hash miss, and the chain n=144-146 exercises positively. Anchor n=41.

desc: evaluate - ex - fail undef: foo => undef evaluates to 0, so a present-but-undefined key is treated as absent
rationale: The row that separates key existence from value definedness: get_input returns undef for both a missing key and an explicitly undefined one (FilterSet.pm:538-547), and filter_ex cannot tell them apart. That is a deliberate flattening — VEP's per-consequence hashes carry undef for unpopulated fields — and it is why n=43 and n=44 are two rows asserting the same answer for two different inputs. Anchor n=41.

desc: evaluate - nex - pass: with the filter `foo nex`, a record lacking foo evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=45-47. filter_nex is `!defined($_[0])` (FilterSet.pm:711), the exact complement of filter_ex, and it is reachable two ways: written out, as here, or produced by finish_filter_node's rewrite of a value-less `ne` (n=15). The family is three rows rather than four because the missing and undefined inputs (n=43/n=44 in the ex family) collapse to the same expectation here. vepyr has no negated existence predicate over annotation fields; see anchor n=41 and file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - nex - fail 0: foo => 0 evaluates to 0, mirroring n=42 — a defined zero is present, so `does not exist` is false for it
rationale: The complement of n=42 and the row that makes the ex/nex pair genuinely exhaustive over the interesting value: if either predicate used truthiness, this row and n=42 would disagree with the pair's stated meaning. Absent in vepyr — anchor n=45.

desc: evaluate - nex - pass undef: foo => undef evaluates to 1, so nex matches a present-but-undefined key exactly as it matches a missing one
rationale: The complement of n=44, and the row that fixes what `nex` means operationally: it selects records where the field carries no usable value, not records where the column is absent from the schema. That distinction is the whole reason a filter language needs nex at all in a format where every consequence hash has the same keys. Anchor n=45.

desc: evaluate - eq - pass: with the filter `foo eq 1`, a record carrying foo => 1 evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=48-52. filter_eq is Perl's *string* comparison, `$_[0] eq $_[1]` (FilterSet.pm:704), even when both operands look numeric — a decision the next four rows probe from both sides. Reaching it, get_input may first rewrite the input: its trailing block (FilterSet.pm:589-610) splits a mixed value like `SIFT(0.02)` into text and number and picks the half that matches the comparison value's shape, which is why the same operator can serve `SIFT eq deleterious` and `SIFT lt 0.05`. vepyr compares no annotation field against a user-supplied operand: header engine grep 0 lines, and the SQL channel is DataFusion's FilterExec rather than vepyr's (0 supports_filters_pushdown overrides against 2 TableProvider impls). no-feature, file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - eq - fail with containing: foo => 11 does NOT match `foo eq 1`, so equality is whole-value and never substring
rationale: The row that distinguishes eq from re (n=99-118), and the one a reimplementation on a CSQ string is most likely to break: grepping an annotated VCF for `1` finds `11`, whereas the filter language compares the *resolved field value* whole. Since VEP's own docs steer users to `re` when they want containment, this row is the boundary between the two operators. Absent in vepyr — anchor n=48.

desc: evaluate - eq - fail 0: foo => 0 does not match `foo eq 1`, the ordinary negative case with a Perl-false input
rationale: Chosen with 0 rather than an arbitrary mismatch so that the negative result cannot come from the input being falsy rather than from the comparison — the same care n=42 takes on the ex side. Anchor n=48.

desc: evaluate - eq - fail missing: a record with no foo key evaluates to 0, by the short-circuit that fires before the predicate runs
rationale: Structurally different from n=50 even though the answer matches: evaluate's guard `if(defined($value) && !defined($input)) { $return = 0 }` (FilterSet.pm:480-482) returns before filter_eq is called at all, so an unresolvable field is never compared against anything. That guard exists only when the filter *has* a value, which is why the ex family (n=43) reaches its 0 by a different route. Anchor n=48.

desc: evaluate - eq - fail undef: foo => undef also evaluates to 0, through the same pre-predicate guard as n=51
rationale: The undefined-value half of the guard at FilterSet.pm:480. Kept as its own row because it pins that the guard tests the *resolved input*, not key existence — had it tested `exists`, this record would have reached filter_eq and warned under `use warnings`. Anchor n=48.

desc: evaluate - ne - pass: with the filter `foo ne 1`, a record carrying foo => 0 evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=53-56. filter_ne is `$_[0] ne $_[1]` (FilterSet.pm:705), the string-inequality mirror of n=48, and the family's real content is the interaction between negation and absence that n=55-56 record. vepyr has no such predicate; see anchor n=41 and file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - ne - fail 0: foo => 1 does not match `foo ne 1` — the ordinary negative case (the Perl test's name says `fail 0`, but the input is 1)
rationale: The direct-hit case, and a naming trap the desc has to step around: the subtest is called `evaluate - ne - fail 0` but its input is foo => 1. Either reading of the name is defensible — `fails, returning 0`, or a copy of the eq family's `fail 0` at t/FilterSet.t:333, which really does pass 0 — so the desc records what the line asserts rather than what it is called, as the desc contract requires. The file does carry at least one certain copy-paste in a subtest name (n=122, labelled `re` inside the nre family), which is a finding about the vendored Perl and never an edit to it. Anchor n=53.

desc: evaluate - ne - fail missing: a record with no foo key evaluates to 0, so `foo ne 1` does NOT select records that lack foo
rationale: The most consequential row of the family and one of the few places VEP's filter language departs from SQL intuition: `ne` is not the complement of `eq`, because the guard at FilterSet.pm:480-482 fires on an unresolvable field for *any* valued operator and returns 0 before the predicate runs. So `Consequence ne missense_variant` silently drops records with no Consequence at all, and expressing `absent or different` needs `nex or ne` written out. A SQL WHERE would answer NULL here and a polars predicate would answer null-propagating false, so even the arithmetic agreement with the SQL channel is coincidental rather than semantic — one more reason the WHERE channel is not an analog-port (see the ledger header). Anchor n=53.

desc: evaluate - ne - fail undef: foo => undef also evaluates to 0, for the same pre-predicate reason as n=55
rationale: The undefined-value half of n=55, and together they make the asymmetry unmissable: of the four ne inputs tested, only a defined non-matching value passes. Anchor n=53.

desc: evaluate - gt - pass: with the filter `foo gt 5`, a record carrying foo => 10 evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=57-68, and the anchor for the four ordered-comparison families n=57-98 as a group. filter_gt is Perl's numeric `>` (FilterSet.pm:706), which numifies both operands, so the same operator serves an integer count, a float allele frequency and a value written in scientific notation without the filter string saying which. Two mechanisms feed it and both are exercised here: get_input's mixed-value split (FilterSet.pm:589-610), which pulls the numeric half out of a value like `deleterious(0.02)` when the comparison operand looks numeric, and evaluate's multi-value branch (:486-497), which splits an &- or comma-joined input and passes if ANY part passes (n=67-68). vepyr applies no user-supplied numeric threshold to an annotation field: the header's engine grep returns 0 lines across all four dfbf crates at 391f94bd against a 562-line positive control, AnnotateVcfConfig's 34 public fields contain no filter knob, and the DataFusion WHERE channel is not vepyr's code (0 supports_filters_pushdown overrides against 2 TableProvider impls). no-feature per the file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - gt - fail 0: foo => 0 does not pass `gt 5`, the ordinary negative with a Perl-false input
rationale: Chosen with 0 so the failure cannot be mistaken for the existence guard rejecting a falsy field — n=42 already established that 0 exists, so reaching filter_gt at all is part of what this row asserts. Anchor n=57.

desc: evaluate - gt - fail match: foo => 5 does not pass `gt 5`, so the comparison is strict
rationale: The boundary row, and the only thing separating this family from n=69-78: gt and gte differ on exactly this input, where n=71 answers 1. A ledger that dropped either row would leave the strict/non-strict distinction unwitnessed. Anchor n=57.

desc: evaluate - gt - fail negative: foo => -1 does not pass `gt 5`, so a leading minus is numified rather than treated as text
rationale: Pins that the operand survives get_input's mixed-value regex intact — its character class `[\w\.\-]` (FilterSet.pm:589) admits the minus, so `-1` is captured whole as the text half rather than split into `-` and `1` — and only then is compared numerically. Contrast n=82, where the same input passes `lt 5`, which is what shows the sign was actually honoured and not merely dropped. Anchor n=57.

desc: evaluate - gt - fail scientific: foo => 1e-5 does not pass `gt 5`, so exponent notation is numified, not string-compared
rationale: Half of the family's scientific-notation pair. If the operands were compared as strings, `1e-05` would sort above `5` and this row would answer 1; it answers 0 because filter_gt is numeric `>`. The `e` is also why get_input's regex admits `e` in both its character classes (FilterSet.pm:589) — otherwise the mixed-value split would corrupt the value before the comparison saw it. Anchor n=57.

desc: evaluate - gt - pass scientific: foo => 1e5 passes `gt 5`, the positive half of the exponent pair
rationale: Read with n=61 it fixes that the exponent's *sign* is honoured — the two inputs differ only by a minus inside the exponent and produce opposite answers, which no string comparison and no truncating parse could reproduce. Anchor n=57.

desc: evaluate - gt - fail decimal: foo => 0.1 does not pass `gt 5`
rationale: First of the decimal pair. Its content beyond n=58 is that a fractional value is compared on its whole magnitude rather than on an integer part: a parse that truncated to 0 would also answer 0 here, which is why the pair needs its other half. Anchor n=57.

desc: evaluate - gt - pass decimal: foo => 5.1 passes `gt 5`, so the fractional part decides the comparison
rationale: The row the decimal pair exists for: 5.1 and 5 have the same integer part and opposite answers (against n=59), so the comparison cannot be truncating. Together with n=61-62 it fixes that VEP's filter language does real numeric comparison over the formats allele frequencies actually arrive in. Anchor n=57.

desc: evaluate - gt - fail missing: a record with no foo key evaluates to 0, through the pre-predicate guard rather than through the comparison
rationale: Same structure as n=51: `if(defined($value) && !defined($input)) { $return = 0 }` (FilterSet.pm:480-482) returns before filter_gt runs, so an unresolvable field is never numified. That ordering is what keeps a missing field from being silently read as 0 and passing `gt -1`. Anchor n=57.

desc: evaluate - gt - fail undef: foo => undef evaluates to 0, through the same guard as n=65
rationale: The undefined-value half. Worth keeping distinct from n=65 because only the guard makes them agree: had the predicate been reached, `undef > 5` would have numified undef to 0 and still answered 0, but with a warning under the `use warnings` this .t enables (t/FilterSet.t:16). Anchor n=57.

desc: evaluate - gt - pass multiple values: foo => '10&15' passes `gt 5`, because the &-joined value is split and ANY part passing is enough
rationale: The family's most important row and the reason VEP's filter language cannot be replaced by a scalar comparison. evaluate's multi-value branch (FilterSet.pm:486-497) fires when the input matches /[0-9](\,|\&)/ — a digit immediately before the delimiter — splits on the delimiter it captured, and reports found if any element satisfies the predicate. That is existential-over-the-multi-value semantics, and it exists because VEP joins per-allele and per-transcript values with & in exactly the fields users filter on. Note the digit gate: `bear&bar` is NOT split (n=102), so &-joined text is matched whole. Anchor n=57.

desc: evaluate - gt - fail multiple values: foo => '1&4' does not pass `gt 5`, because no part of the split passes
rationale: The negative half of n=67, and the row that proves the split is existential rather than merely permissive: both elements are compared and both fail, so the answer is 0 rather than the 1 a short-circuit-on-first-element or a compare-the-whole-string implementation would give. Anchor n=57.

desc: evaluate - gte - pass: with the filter `foo gte 5`, a record carrying foo => 10 evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=69-78. filter_gte is numeric `>=` (FilterSet.pm:708), reached through the same get_input and multi-value machinery as gt; the family repeats gt's ten scalar cases so that the strict/non-strict boundary is witnessed on both sides rather than inferred. It has ten rows to gt's twelve because the &-split pair is not repeated here — a coverage gap upstream rather than a semantic difference, since the branch at FilterSet.pm:487 is operator-agnostic. Absent in vepyr for the reason given at the ordered-comparison anchor n=57 and the file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - gte - fail 0: foo => 0 does not pass `gte 5`
rationale: The ordinary negative, with 0 chosen for the same reason as n=58: the failure must come from the comparison, not from the field being read as absent. Anchor n=69.

desc: evaluate - gte - pass match: foo => 5 DOES pass `gte 5` — the one input on which this family differs from gt
rationale: The row the whole family exists for. Against n=59, which answers 0 on the identical input, it is the only evidence in the corpus that `>=` was not implemented as `>`; every other row of the two families agrees. Anchor n=69.

desc: evaluate - gte - fail negative: foo => -1 does not pass `gte 5`
rationale: The sign case at the non-strict operator, mirroring n=60. Paired with n=92 (`-1` passes `lte 5`) it shows the minus is honoured under both directions of the comparison rather than only where it happens to be harmless. Anchor n=69.

desc: evaluate - gte - fail scientific: foo => 1e-5 does not pass `gte 5`
rationale: Exponent notation at the non-strict operator; without it the family would leave open whether gte shares gt's numification path or has its own. Anchor n=69.

desc: evaluate - gte - pass scientific: foo => 1e5 passes `gte 5`
rationale: The positive exponent half, completing the pair with n=73 exactly as n=61-62 do for gt. Anchor n=69.

desc: evaluate - gte - fail decimal: foo => 0.1 does not pass `gte 5`
rationale: The fractional negative. Its pairing with n=76 is what rules out a truncating parse for this operator, the same argument n=63-64 make for gt. Anchor n=69.

desc: evaluate - gte - pass decimal: foo => 5.1 passes `gte 5`
rationale: The fractional positive, and against n=71 it also shows the non-strict operator is not simply `==` widened: 5.1 and 5 both pass, for different reasons. Anchor n=69.

desc: evaluate - gte - fail missing: a record with no foo key evaluates to 0, through the pre-predicate guard
rationale: The absence case for the non-strict operator. It matters more here than at n=65 because `gte` is the operator a user reaches for when they want `at least`, and a missing field numifying to 0 would pass `gte 0` — the guard at FilterSet.pm:480-482 is what stops it. Anchor n=69.

desc: evaluate - gte - fail undef: foo => undef evaluates to 0, through the same guard as n=77
rationale: The present-but-undefined half, kept distinct for the reason given at n=66: the guard, not the comparison, is what produces the answer. Anchor n=69.

desc: evaluate - lt - pass: with the filter `foo lt 5`, a record carrying foo => 1 evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=79-88. filter_lt is numeric `<` (FilterSet.pm:707). The family is not a mirror image of gt's: because the threshold sits above most of the probe values, the pass/fail polarity of every shared input flips, which is what makes the pair a real test of the comparison rather than of one direction of it. This is also the operator users reach for most in practice — `gnomADe_AF lt 0.01` — so the decimal and exponent rows below carry the family's practical weight. Absent in vepyr; see the ordered-comparison anchor n=57 and the file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - lt - pass 0: foo => 0 passes `lt 5`, the input that fails in both gt families
rationale: The polarity flip stated plainly: the same record that answers 0 at n=58 and n=70 answers 1 here. Together the three rows show the operand is compared, not merely tested for truth — a filter language built on truthiness would answer identically for all three. Anchor n=79.

desc: evaluate - lt - fail match: foo => 5 does not pass `lt 5`, so this comparison is strict too
rationale: The boundary row of the lower half, and the counterpart of n=59: it is what n=91 contradicts on the identical input to separate lt from lte. Anchor n=79.

desc: evaluate - lt - pass negative: foo => -1 passes `lt 5`, so the minus sign is honoured rather than stripped
rationale: The positive control for n=60, and the stronger of the two: at n=60 an implementation that dropped the sign would still answer 0 by accident, whereas here dropping it would give `1 < 5` — the same answer again — but *reversing* it would not. Read with n=72, where -1 fails `gte 5`, the three rows fix the sign's effect under both directions. Anchor n=79.

desc: evaluate - lt - fail scientific: foo => 1e5 does not pass `lt 5`
rationale: Note the operand swap against the gt family: here the *large* exponent is the failing case, so the pair n=83-84 is not a copy of n=61-62 with the answers negated but a re-derivation on inputs chosen for this direction. Anchor n=79.

desc: evaluate - lt - pass scientific: foo => 1e-5 passes `lt 5`
rationale: The case that matters in real use: allele frequencies arrive from the cache in exponent form, and `AF lt 0.01` has to accept `1e-05`. If exponent notation were compared as text, `1e-05` would sort above `5` and this row would fail. Anchor n=79.

desc: evaluate - lt - fail decimal: foo => 5.1 does not pass `lt 5`
rationale: The fractional negative for this direction; against n=81 it shows the fractional part is what decides, since the integer parts are equal. Anchor n=79.

desc: evaluate - lt - pass decimal: foo => 0.1 passes `lt 5`
rationale: The fractional positive, completing the pair with n=85 and matching the practical shape of `lt` filters over frequencies. Anchor n=79.

desc: evaluate - lt - fail missing: a record with no foo key evaluates to 0, NOT 1 — absence does not satisfy a `less than` filter
rationale: The most consequential absence row of the four ordered families. Numifying a missing field to 0 would make it pass every `lt` with a positive threshold, so `gnomADe_AF lt 0.01` would select every variant with no frequency data at all — exactly the wrong answer for a rare-variant filter. The guard at FilterSet.pm:480-482 is what prevents it, and this row is where that behaviour is pinned. Anchor n=79.

desc: evaluate - lt - fail undef: foo => undef evaluates to 0, through the same guard as n=87
rationale: The present-but-undefined half of n=87, and the common case in practice: VEP's per-consequence hashes carry the key with an undefined value for variants absent from the frequency source, so this is the row that actually fires on real data. Anchor n=79.

desc: evaluate - lte - pass: with the filter `foo lte 5`, a record carrying foo => 1 evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=89-98. filter_lte is numeric `<=` (FilterSet.pm:709), the last of the four ordered comparisons, and the family completes the 2x2 of direction (gt/lt) against strictness (gt/gte, lt/lte) that n=57-98 exist to pin. Ten rows, the same scalar cases as gte, and again no &-split pair — the multi-value branch is operator-agnostic and is exercised once, at n=67-68. Absent in vepyr; see the ordered-comparison anchor n=57 and the file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - lte - pass 0: foo => 0 passes `lte 5`
rationale: The falsy-input pass, mirroring n=80 at the non-strict operator. Anchor n=89.

desc: evaluate - lte - pass match: foo => 5 DOES pass `lte 5` — the input on which this family differs from lt
rationale: The row the family exists for, and the fourth corner of the 2x2: against n=81, which answers 0 on the identical input, it is the only evidence that `<=` was not implemented as `<`. With n=71 it also confirms the two non-strict operators are non-strict in the same way. Anchor n=89.

desc: evaluate - lte - pass negative: foo => -1 passes `lte 5`
rationale: The sign case for the non-strict lower comparison, and the fourth reading of `-1` across the four families (n=60 fail, n=72 fail, n=82 pass, here pass) — a set that no sign-dropping or absolute-value implementation could reproduce. Anchor n=89.

desc: evaluate - lte - fail scientific: foo => 1e5 does not pass `lte 5`
rationale: The large-exponent negative for this direction, mirroring n=83. Anchor n=89.

desc: evaluate - lte - pass scientific: foo => 1e-5 passes `lte 5`
rationale: The small-exponent positive, mirroring n=84 and carrying the same practical weight for frequency filters written with `<=`. Anchor n=89.

desc: evaluate - lte - fail decimal: foo => 5.1 does not pass `lte 5`
rationale: The fractional negative just above the threshold; against n=91 it shows that the non-strict operator admits equality without admitting anything above it. Anchor n=89.

desc: evaluate - lte - pass decimal: foo => 0.1 passes `lte 5`
rationale: The fractional positive, closing the family's decimal pair. Anchor n=89.

desc: evaluate - lte - fail missing: a record with no foo key evaluates to 0, not 1
rationale: The absence case at the operator where a wrong answer would be most damaging, for the reason spelled out at n=87: `lte` with a positive threshold is the shape of a rare-variant filter, and a missing field numified to 0 would pass every one of them. Anchor n=89.

desc: evaluate - lte - fail undef: foo => undef evaluates to 0, through the same guard as n=97
rationale: The present-but-undefined half, and the last of the eight absence rows across n=57-98. All eight answer 0, by the guard rather than by the comparison, which is the single most reusable fact about this operator group. Anchor n=89.

desc: evaluate - re - pass match: with the filter `foo re bar`, a record carrying foo => 'bar' evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=99-118, the largest family in the file. filter_re is `$_[0] =~ /$_[1]/i` (FilterSet.pm:714): the operand is interpolated into the pattern position, so it is a *regular expression*, not a literal, and the /i flag makes every match case-insensitive whether the user wanted that or not. Twenty rows fall out of that one line — seven for the plain-substring behaviour (n=99-105) and thirteen for four metacharacter classes given their own constructor: `.` (n=106-108), `.*` (n=109-111), `.+` (n=112-114) and a character set (n=115-118). Also reachable as the aliases `match`, `matches` and `regex` (%FILTER_SYNONYMS, FilterSet.pm:114-116). vepyr matches no user-supplied pattern against an annotation field: the header's engine grep returns 0 lines across all four dfbf crates at 391f94bd against a 562-line positive control, and a WHERE ... LIKE or regexp_match over annotate_vep() output would be DataFusion's regex engine under test, not vepyr's (0 supports_filters_pushdown overrides against 2 TableProvider impls). no-feature per the file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - re - pass part match 1: foo => 'bare' matches `re bar`, so the pattern is unanchored at the end
rationale: First half of the containment pair. The pattern is interpolated without \A or \z (FilterSet.pm:714), so a trailing suffix on the data does not defeat the match — which is exactly what makes `re` the operator VEP's documentation points users at when `eq` is too strict (see n=49, where `foo eq 1` refuses `11`). Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - pass part match 2: foo => 'ebar' matches `re bar`, so the pattern is unanchored at the start too
rationale: The other half of the containment pair, and it is a separate claim rather than a symmetry: a naive implementation using an anchored prefix match would satisfy n=100 and fail here. Together the two rows fix that `re` is substring-by-default. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - pass with & character: foo => 'bear&bar' matches `re bar` — the &-joined value is matched WHOLE, not split
rationale: The row that fixes the boundary of the multi-value split at n=67. evaluate's split branch is gated on /[0-9](\,|\&)/ (FilterSet.pm:487) — a **digit** immediately before the delimiter — so `bear&bar`, whose & follows a letter, never enters it and is matched as one string. The distinction is not cosmetic: VEP joins Consequence terms with & (`missense_variant&splice_region_variant`), and because those parts are alphabetic the whole field is regex-matched, which is precisely why `Consequence re missense` works while `Consequence eq missense_variant` does not (n=27, n=49). Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - fail: foo => 'bear' does not match `re bar`, so containment is over the literal character sequence
rationale: The family's negative control, chosen as a near-miss anagram rather than an obviously different word: it shares every character of the pattern but not their order, so the row rules out a set-of-characters or fuzzy implementation that would still satisfy n=99-102. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - fail missing: a record with no foo key evaluates to 0, through the pre-predicate guard rather than through a failed match
rationale: Same guard as n=51 and n=65 (FilterSet.pm:480-482), and it matters here because the alternative is a warning rather than a wrong answer: `undef =~ /bar/i` would answer false anyway, but noisily under the `use warnings` this .t enables. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - fail undef: foo => undef evaluates to 0, through the same guard as n=104
rationale: The present-but-undefined half. Kept distinct for the reason given throughout the evaluate families: absence and undefinedness reach the same answer by the same route, and the ledger records both because the Perl asserts both. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - . wildcard - pass: with `foo re b.r`, foo => 'bar' matches — the operand really is compiled as a regex, not quoted
rationale: The decisive row of the whole family: if the operand were escaped with \Q or compared as a literal, `b.r` could never match `bar`, and n=99-105 would all still pass. This is where the ledger records that VEP's filter language exposes Perl's regex engine directly to the filter string — a design decision with real consequences (an unescaped user operand, and Perl-dialect patterns) that a Rust reimplementation would have to make deliberately. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - . wildcard - fail no char: foo => 'br' does not match `b.r`, so `.` requires exactly one character
rationale: The lower bound of `.`, and the row that separates it from `.*` (n=110 answers 1 on this identical input). Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - . wildcard - fail >1 char: foo => 'baar' does not match `b.r`, so `.` matches exactly one character and the pattern is not implicitly padded
rationale: The upper bound of `.`. Combined with n=107 it pins the quantifier exactly, and against n=111 and n=114 — which both answer 1 on this input — it is what makes the three wildcard sub-families genuinely distinct. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - .* wildcard - pass: with `foo re b.*r`, foo => 'bar' matches
rationale: The one-character case of the zero-or-more quantifier, and the input all three wildcard sub-families share so their answers can be compared row for row (n=106, n=109, n=112 all answer 1). Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - .* wildcard - pass no char: foo => 'br' matches `b.*r`, so `*` admits zero occurrences
rationale: The row that distinguishes `.*` from `.` (n=107) and from `.+` (n=113), both of which answer 0 on this identical input. Three rows over one input is how the family pins quantifier semantics without a single assertion about the regex engine itself. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - .* wildcard - pass >1 char: foo => 'baar' matches `b.*r`, so `*` admits more than one occurrence
rationale: The upper end of the quantifier, against n=108's 0 on the same input. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - .+ wildcard - pass: with `foo re b.+r`, foo => 'bar' matches
rationale: The one-character case of the one-or-more quantifier — the case where `.`, `.*` and `.+` all agree, which is what makes n=113 and n=114 the informative rows of this sub-family. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - .+ wildcard - fail no char: foo => 'br' does not match `b.+r`, so `+` requires at least one occurrence
rationale: The row that separates `+` from `*`: n=110 answers 1 on this identical input. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - .+ wildcard - pass >1 char: foo => 'baar' matches `b.+r`, so `+` is unbounded above
rationale: Completes the three-quantifier table over the two boundary inputs `br` and `baar`: `.` gives (0,0), `.*` gives (1,1), `.+` gives (0,1). No two quantifiers share a row of that table, which is what the eight rows n=107-114 buy. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - charset - pass: with `foo re b[abcde]r`, foo => 'bar' matches, so bracketed character sets survive interpolation intact
rationale: The fourth metacharacter class, and the one that shows the operand is passed through with no escaping of any kind: `[`, `]` and the enumerated alternatives all reach the regex engine as syntax. That the filter string can contain brackets at all also depends on the parser's scanner, whose word class excludes only parentheses and whitespace (FilterSet.pm:223) — brackets are ordinary word characters to it. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - charset - fail no char: foo => 'br' does not match `b[abcde]r`, so a character set is a one-character quantifier
rationale: The lower bound, matching `.`'s behaviour at n=107 and confirming that the set is not implicitly optional. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - charset - fail char not in set: foo => 'byr' does not match `b[abcde]r`, so membership is actually enforced
rationale: The row the character-set sub-family exists for: without it, a `.`-like implementation that ignored the bracket contents would satisfy n=115 and n=116. `y` is chosen as a letter, so the failure cannot be explained by a class/type distinction. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - re - charset - fail num: foo => 'b1r' does not match `b[abcde]r`, so a digit is not admitted by a letter set
rationale: The second membership negative, with a digit rather than a letter. Its value beyond n=117 is that it rules out any numeric coercion sneaking in before the match — get_input's mixed-value block (FilterSet.pm:589-610) does inspect values that contain digits, and this row confirms the input still reaches the regex as the string `b1r`. Anchor n=99.

desc: evaluate - nre - pass: with the filter `foo nre bar`, a record carrying foo => 'car' evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=119-125. filter_nre is `$_[0] !~ /$_[1]/i` (FilterSet.pm:715), the negation of n=99's predicate with the same interpolation and the same /i. Seven rows, mirroring the plain-substring half of the re family exactly — the metacharacter sub-families are not repeated, which is an upstream coverage choice rather than a semantic difference, since both predicates compile the operand identically. The family's own content is the absence asymmetry at n=124-125. Absent in vepyr; see anchor n=99 and file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - nre - fail part match 1: foo => 'bare' does not pass `nre bar`, because the substring is present
rationale: The negation of n=100, and the row that confirms nre inherits re's unanchored-at-the-end behaviour rather than being anchored equality-negation. Anchor n=119.

desc: evaluate - nre - fail part match 2: foo => 'ebar' does not pass `nre bar`, unanchored at the start as well
rationale: The negation of n=101, completing the containment pair on the negative operator. Anchor n=119.

desc: evaluate - nre - fail with & character: foo => 'bear&bar' does not pass `nre bar`, because the &-joined value is matched whole and does contain the pattern
rationale: The negation of n=102, and the row where the vendored Perl's subtest name is certainly a copy-paste: t/FilterSet.t:434 is labelled `evaluate - re - fail with & character` while sitting inside the nre block and constructing `foo nre bar` at :430. The desc records what the line asserts, per the desc contract; the label is a finding about the vendored file and never an edit to it (t/FilterSet.t is byte-identical to upstream, sha256 pinned in this ledger's header). The behaviour itself matters for real filters: `Consequence nre missense` rejects `missense_variant&splice_region_variant` because the digit gate at FilterSet.pm:487 leaves alphabetic &-joins unsplit. Anchor n=119.

desc: evaluate - nre - pass near match: foo => 'bear' passes `nre bar`, the negation of the family's near-miss control
rationale: The mirror of n=103: the same near-anagram input, the opposite answer, which is what shows nre is the complement of re over the *matching* inputs rather than a separately implemented predicate. Anchor n=119.

desc: evaluate - nre - fail missing: a record with no foo key evaluates to 0 — `does not match` is FALSE for a field that is not there
rationale: The family's most consequential row, and the exact analogue of n=55 for the regex operators: because the guard at FilterSet.pm:480-482 fires for any valued operator before the predicate runs, nre is *not* the complement of re over all inputs — both answer 0 on a missing field. So `--filter "Consequence nre missense"` silently drops records with no Consequence, and expressing `absent or non-matching` needs `nex or nre` written out. This is also where the SQL-channel comparison finally breaks even arithmetically: `NOT (col ~ 'missense')` over a NULL is NULL, not false. Anchor n=119.

desc: evaluate - nre - fail undef: foo => undef also evaluates to 0, through the same guard as n=124
rationale: The present-but-undefined half of n=124 and the common case on real data, where VEP's per-consequence hashes carry the key with an undefined value rather than omitting it. Anchor n=119.

desc: evaluate - in list - pass 1: with the filter `foo in 1,2`, a record carrying foo => 1 evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=126-130. filter_in is `exists($_[1]->{$_[0]})` (FilterSet.pm:718) — a hash-membership test, not a scan — which works only because finish_filter_node already turned the comma list into a lookup hash at parse time (n=19). So the operand of `in` has a different runtime type from every other operator's, and evaluate reaches it through the same `$filter->{value}` slot: get_input even has a special case for it, picking an arbitrary key when it needs a scalar to decide the mixed-value split (`if (ref $value eq "HASH") { $value = (keys %{$value})[0] }`, FilterSet.pm:597-599). vepyr tests no annotation field for membership in a user-supplied set: header engine grep 0 lines across four dfbf crates at 391f94bd, 562-line positive control, and no set-valued knob among AnnotateVcfConfig's 34 public fields. no-feature per the file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - in list - pass 2: foo => 2 also evaluates to 1, so membership holds for every element of the list rather than only the first
rationale: The second element, and a real claim rather than a duplicate: an implementation that compared against `(keys %$value)[0]` — the very scalar get_input takes for its own purposes at FilterSet.pm:580 — would satisfy n=126 and fail here. Anchor n=126.

desc: evaluate - in list - fail: foo => 3 evaluates to 0, so membership is exact and the set is closed
rationale: The negative, and note the input is adjacent to the set (3 next to 1,2) rather than arbitrary, so it also rules out a range reading of the comma list. Anchor n=126.

desc: evaluate - in list - fail missing: a record with no foo key evaluates to 0, through the pre-predicate guard
rationale: The guard at FilterSet.pm:480-482 again, and here it prevents something specific: `exists($_[1]->{undef})` would stringify undef to the empty string and test for a key named '' — silently true for any list containing an empty element, which a file-backed set with a trailing blank line easily has (n=131). Anchor n=126.

desc: evaluate - in list - fail undef: foo => undef evaluates to 0, through the same guard as n=129
rationale: The present-but-undefined half, closing the list sub-family's absence pair. Anchor n=126.

desc: evaluate - in file - pass 1: with the filter `foo in <VEPTestingConfig filter_list path>`, a record carrying foo => 'MRPL39' evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=131-135. Same predicate as n=126 and deliberately so: the file was read and hashed at parse time by finish_filter_node (n=20), so evaluate touches no filesystem and cannot tell a file-backed set from a literal one. What the sub-family adds is the end-to-end proof that the two operand forms are interchangeable at evaluation — the property that makes `--filter "SYMBOL in genes.txt"` the standard way to run a gene panel, which is the single most common real-world use of this operator. vepyr reads no gene list: header engine grep 0 lines across four dfbf crates, and no list-file path among AnnotateVcfConfig's 34 public fields or the 31-key DataFusion option vocabulary. no-feature, file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - in file - pass 2: foo => 'JAM2' also evaluates to 1, the file's second entry
rationale: The second line of the fixture, and it carries the same weight here as n=127 does for the literal list: it is what shows the whole file was hashed rather than only its first line. Anchor n=131.

desc: evaluate - in file - fail: foo => 3 evaluates to 0 — a value absent from the file, and of a different type from its entries
rationale: The negative for the file form. The input is numeric while the set holds gene symbols, which also confirms filter_in does no coercion: the hash lookup stringifies and misses, rather than the mixed-value machinery at FilterSet.pm:589-610 turning either side into the other's type. Anchor n=131.

desc: evaluate - in file - fail missing: a record with no foo key evaluates to 0, through the pre-predicate guard
rationale: The absence case for the file form, and the one where the guard earns its keep most visibly: a gene list read line by line can end with a blank line, giving the set a '' key (FilterSet.pm:396-412 adds whatever chomp leaves), and without the guard an undef input would stringify to '' and match it. Anchor n=131.

desc: evaluate - in file - fail undef: foo => undef evaluates to 0, through the same guard as n=134
rationale: The present-but-undefined half, and the last of the ten `in` rows. Across n=126-135 the two operand forms agree on all five inputs, which is the sub-families' joint claim. Anchor n=131.

desc: evaluate - and - pass: with the filter `foo and bar`, a record carrying both keys evaluates to 1
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=136-143, the three rows-groups that pin how evaluate *combines* results rather than how it computes one. A node with children seeds an accumulator at 1 and folds its children left to right — `$return *= $value` for a child whose logic is 'and', `$return += $value` for 'or' (FilterSet.pm:454-459) — and a node's `not` flag inverts the reduced result afterwards (:507-508). There is no precedence table and no short-circuit: every child is evaluated. This row is the conjunctive identity case, 1*1*1. vepyr composes no per-record predicates: the header's engine grep returns 0 lines across all four dfbf crates at 391f94bd against a 562-line positive control, and boolean composition over annotate_vep() output would be DataFusion's LogicalPlan, not vepyr's code (0 supports_filters_pushdown overrides against 2 TableProvider impls). no-feature per the file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - and - fail: `foo and bar` with only foo present evaluates to 0, because the multiplicative fold zeroes on the missing conjunct
rationale: The conjunctive negative, and it shows the fold is arithmetic rather than boolean: filter_ex returns Perl's empty string for the absent `bar`, and it is the multiplication at FilterSet.pm:455 that turns it into 0. That coercion point matters for n=138, where the additive branch turns the same values into 2. Anchor n=136.

desc: evaluate - or - pass 1: `foo or bar` with BOTH keys present evaluates to 2, not 1 — evaluate returns a count, not a boolean
rationale: The single most surprising assertion in the file, and the reason n=29's parse-tree fact matters. Because `or` adds (FilterSet.pm:458) and the accumulator starts at 1, a two-branch disjunction with both branches true returns 2. filter_vep only ever tests the result for truth, so the excess is invisible there — but it is part of the contract this ledger records, and any reimplementation returning a bool would fail this row while passing n=139 and n=140. It also fixes that there is no short-circuit: the second branch is evaluated even though the first already passed. Anchor n=136.

desc: evaluate - or - pass 2: `foo or bar` with only foo present evaluates to 1
rationale: The ordinary disjunctive pass: 1*1 for the first child, then += the empty string for the second, which numifies to 0 and leaves 1. Read with n=138 it shows the return value counts satisfied branches. Anchor n=136.

desc: evaluate - or - fail: `foo or bar` against a record whose only key is `goo` evaluates to 0
rationale: The disjunctive negative, and it quietly exercises the synonym search's *substring* arm: get_input's last resort is `grep {$_ =~ /^$field/i} keys %$data` (FilterSet.pm:568), and `goo` does not begin with `foo` or `bar`, so nothing is found. Had the fixture used `food` the answer would have been different — which is why the row's input is worth reading rather than skimming. Anchor n=136.

desc: evaluate - not - pass: with the filter `not foo`, a record lacking foo evaluates to 1
rationale: The negation flag n=23 placed on the node, now read at evaluation time: FilterSet.pm:507-508 inverts the *reduced* value with `$return == 0 ? 1 : 0`, i.e. numerically, which is what normalises filter_ex's empty string into a clean 1. Note the inversion happens per node, after the fold, so `not` over a group inverts the group's whole result (n=33) rather than distributing over its children. Anchor n=136.

desc: evaluate - not - pass undef: `not foo` with foo => undef also evaluates to 1, since the inner existence test failed
rationale: The present-but-undefined case, inherited from n=44's flattening of absence and undefinedness. It confirms `not` is a pure inversion of what the inner node returned rather than a separately-computed absence test. Anchor n=136.

desc: evaluate - not - fail: `not foo` with foo => 1 evaluates to 0
rationale: The inversion's other direction, and the row that makes the numeric normalisation visible: the inner node returns 1, `1 == 0` is false, so the ternary yields 0 rather than Perl's `!1` empty string — which the root's multiplication would then have coerced anyway, but the ledger records what the code does, not what would have been survivable. Anchor n=136.

desc: evaluate - synonym - uc: the filter `foo` matches a record whose key is FOO, resolving the field name case-insensitively upwards
rationale: FAMILY ANCHOR for n=144-152, the field-name resolution layer. get_input (FilterSet.pm:533-613) does not look a field up once: it tries the literal key, then a memoised synonym, then lc, then uc, then a "_"-prefixed variant, and finally a case-insensitive *prefix* match over the record's keys, throwing if that last arm is ambiguous (:573-580). Each hit is memoised in the synonyms hash so later records skip the search. This row pins the uc arm. It also corrects detailed_plans/FilterSet.md, which calls this SO synonym matching: it is field-NAME resolution over the data hash's own keys and involves no ontology at all. vepyr resolves no user-supplied field name against its output schema — the CSQ field list is fixed by the header it writes — and the header's engine grep (0 lines across four dfbf crates at 391f94bd, 562-line positive control) covers limit_synonym_search by name. no-feature per the file anchor n=2.

desc: evaluate - synonym - lc: the filter `FOO` matches a record whose key is foo, the downward direction
rationale: The lc arm (FilterSet.pm:552-555), and a separate claim from n=144 because the two arms are tried in a fixed order — lc first — which decides the winner when a record carries both spellings. Anchor n=144.

desc: evaluate - synonym - underscore: the filter `foo` matches a record whose key is _foo, so a leading underscore is transparent to the filter language
